card vi-sysdiag-derive  [decided]
Nodes are folded from the cards by an agent. Edges come from the cards, once decided. The text is cached
why: Cards name the parts of the product but not the arrows between them, so the fold reads two sources — see #vi-sysdiag-edges. Reading cards into parts needs interpretation, not a data transformation. An agent read is slow and non-deterministic, so it cannot run on every view; the resolution is #vi-images' split, where the diagram text is cached and the render is not.
subtree: 10 cards, 1 open, 4 proto, 5 decided

Four claims.

**1. The node fold needs judgement.** No projection of card fields yields a component. #vi-graph3d decides a view; #werk-hmr decides a dev loop; #vi-edges decides a data shape. Only a reader can tell which is a part of the product, and at which level. The sort that makes this possible is #vi-sysdiag-classes.

**2. Edges come from the cards, once a card decides them — not from the code.** #vi-sysdiag-edges tried reading arrows from the prototype code. That was wrong: the code's shape is an accident, not a decision, per #vi-sysdiag-purpose. Reading it in would hide the gap where a decision is still missing. A missing arrow is a question to answer, per #vi-sysdiag-ask, not data to fetch.

**3. So the diagram text is a cached artifact, not a view.** It is a peer of the card text — stored, diffed, edited in place. The picture drawn from it stays disposable, per #vi-images.

First, a trap to avoid. A depends_on edge between two cards is not an arrow between two parts.

#werk-shots depends_on #werk-pane. That means the screenshot decision needed the pane decision first. It does not mean the screenshot code calls the pane. Same word, two graphs, two meanings.

Second, what the empty arrows mean. We decided what the parts are. We never decided how they talk. The diagram makes that visible for the first time. An empty arrow is a question to answer, not data to fetch — see #vi-sysdiag-ask.

So the arrows come from the cards, once the cards exist. Reading them out of the prototype code would hide the gap instead of showing it.

=== vi-sysdiag-grain
card vi-sysdiag-grain  [decided]
One diagram file. Redraw it whole each turn, with the old drawing in context
why: The scope of a redraw is a judgement, not a lookup. Given the changed card and the whole current diagram, the agent can see whether this is a renamed box or a wrong grouping, and choose a minimal edit or a rethink. A fine-grained dirty mark hands it the answer to that question before it asks it.
subtree: 2 cards, 1 proto, 1 decided

With no resource limit you would redraw from scratch every time. The old drawing is then not a saving, it is an input — it is what makes the new drawing continuous with the reader's mental model.

So the grain question was posed wrong. It is not "which storage shape is cheaper". It is "is the scope of the redraw mechanical or judged". Judged. One file, rewritten whole, with the previous file in the prompt.

What this costs: the redraw can silently restructure. The reader cannot tell a moved box from a rethought boundary. That has to be declared — see #vi-sysdiag-declare.

Where it stops holding: this works because a forty-node diagram and its card set fit in one read. Nothing needs recovering, so #vi-prop's 6% to 11% does not apply. Past that size the marked-set mechanism comes back — see #vi-sysdiag-backedge.

  -> refines         vi-sysdiag-backedge  The card ids on the diagram are a hint now. They become the mechanism when the diagram outgrows one read
